narrative: Your promotion was denied because the model flagged you as a leave risk: it estimates a 44% probability that you will leave, meaning there is a substantial—though not certain—chance you may exit. The three strongest factors were training in the last three years, your tenure in the current organization, and your total experience. The most influential factor was your extensive training: having attended seven or more programs in three years pushed your risk toward staying, and only about one in five employees predicted to stay had that much training. However, the next two factors pushed toward leaving and outweighed that positive signal. Your one-to-five years in this organization was the second-ranked factor and raised leave risk; although about half of stayers also have this tenure, in your profile it suggests you may be at a stage where internal progression matters. Your six-to-ten years of overall experience was third and also pushed toward leaving; this is less common among stayers, about a third of whom share it. Before treating this as a final judgment, the organization should use it as a retention warning: discuss your career path and promotion criteria, keep using development and training as an engagement lever, and review workload, overtime, pay, and stress supports. You should ask for clear milestones and a follow-up review.
